claim: Telomeres are chromosomal end structures that play a crucial role in maintaining genome stability and integrity in eukaryotes.
source: Telomeres, which are chromosomal end structures, play a crucial role in maintaining genome stability and integrity in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in telomere biology supported by extensive scientific literature.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, X-elements are found in all 32 telomeres.
source: In the baker's yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the X- and Y'-elements are subtelomeric repetitive sequences found in all 32 and 17 telomeres, respectively.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characteristic of S. cerevisiae telomere structure.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Y'-elements are found in 17 telomeres.
source: In the baker's yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the X- and Y'-elements are subtelomeric repetitive sequences found in all 32 and 17 telomeres, respectively.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characteristic of S. cerevisiae telomere structure.

claim: Y'-elements serve as a backup for telomere functions in cells lacking telomerase.
source: While the Y'-elements serve as a backup for telomere functions in cells lacking telomerase, the function of the X-elements remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by references to previous studies on telomerase-null survivors.

claim: The function of X-elements remains unclear.
source: While the Y'-elements serve as a backup for telomere functions in cells lacking telomerase, the function of the X-elements remains unclear.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a knowledge gap.

claim: The SY12 strain has three chromosomes and six telomeres.
source: This study utilized the S. cerevisiae strain SY12, which has three chromosomes and six telomeres, to investigate the role of X-elements (as well as Y'-elements) in telomere maintenance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and confirmed by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of Y'-elements in SY12 (SY12YΔ) did not impact the length of terminal TG1-3 tracks.
source: Deletion of Y'-elements (SY12YΔ), X-elements (SY12XYΔ+Y), or both X- and Y'-elements (SY12XYΔ) did not impact the length of the terminal TG1-3 tracks or telomere silencing.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by Southern blotting data in Figure 4A.

claim: Deletion of X-elements in SY12 (SY12XYΔ+Y) did not impact the length of terminal TG1-3 tracks.
source: Deletion of Y'-elements (SY12YΔ), X-elements (SY12XYΔ+Y), or both X- and Y'-elements (SY12XYΔ) did not impact the length of the terminal TG1-3 tracks or telomere silencing.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by Southern blotting data in Figure 4A.

claim: Deletion of both X- and Y'-elements in SY12 (SY12XYΔ) did not impact the length of terminal TG1-3 tracks.
source: Deletion of Y'-elements (SY12YΔ), X-elements (SY12XYΔ+Y), or both X- and Y'-elements (SY12XYΔ) did not impact the length of the terminal TG1-3 tracks or telomere silencing.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by Southern blotting data in Figure 4A.

claim: Deletion of Y'-elements, X-elements, or both did not impact telomere silencing in SY12.
source: Deletion of Y'-elements (SY12YΔ), X-elements (SY12XYΔ+Y), or both X- and Y'-elements (SY12XYΔ) did not impact the length of the terminal TG1-3 tracks or telomere silencing.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4B.

claim: Inactivation of telomerase in SY12YΔ cells resulted in cellular senescence and the generation of survivors.
source: However, inactivation of telomerase in SY12YΔ, SY12XYΔ+Y, and SY12XYΔ cells resulted in cellular senescence and the generation of survivors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cell viability assays and Southern blotting data in Figure 5.

claim: Inactivation of telomerase in SY12XYΔ+Y cells resulted in cellular senescence and the generation of survivors.
source: However, inactivation of telomerase in SY12YΔ, SY12XYΔ+Y, and SY12XYΔ cells resulted in cellular senescence and the generation of survivors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cell viability assays and Southern blotting data in Figure 6.

claim: Inactivation of telomerase in SY12XYΔ cells resulted in cellular senescence and the generation of survivors.
source: However, inactivation of telomerase in SY12YΔ, SY12XYΔ+Y, and SY12XYΔ cells resulted in cellular senescence and the generation of survivors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cell viability assays and Southern blotting data in Figure 6.

claim: Survivors from telomerase-null SY12 derivative strains maintained their telomeres through homologous recombination-dependent TG1-3 track elongation.
source: These survivors either maintained their telomeres through homologous recombination-dependent TG1-3 track elongation or underwent microhomology-mediated intra-chromosomal end-to-end joining.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Southern blotting and sequencing data throughout the Results section.

claim: Survivors from telomerase-null SY12 derivative strains underwent microhomology-mediated intra-chromosomal end-to-end joining.
source: These survivors either maintained their telomeres through homologous recombination-dependent TG1-3 track elongation or underwent microhomology-mediated intra-chromosomal end-to-end joining.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by PCR-sequencing data in Figures 2F, 5E, and 6D,F.

claim: Subtelomeric X- and Y'-elements are non-essential for telomere regulation in telomerase-proficient cells.
source: Our findings indicate the non-essential role of subtelomeric X- and Y'-elements in telomere regulation in both telomerase-proficient and telomerase-null cells and suggest that these elements may represent remnants of S. cerevisiae genome evolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 3 and 4 showing normal cell growth and telomere maintenance.

claim: Subtelomeric X- and Y'-elements are non-essential for telomere regulation in telomerase-null cells.
source: Our findings indicate the non-essential role of subtelomeric X- and Y'-elements in telomere regulation in both telomerase-proficient and telomerase-null cells and suggest that these elements may represent remnants of S. cerevisiae genome evolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by data showing survivor formation in strains lacking these elements (Figures 5 and 6).

claim: X- and Y'-elements may represent remnants of S. cerevisiae genome evolution.
source: Our findings indicate the non-essential role of subtelomeric X- and Y'-elements in telomere regulation in both telomerase-proficient and telomerase-null cells and suggest that these elements may represent remnants of S. cerevisiae genome evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the finding that these elements are dispensable for essential telomere functions.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, telomeric DNA consists of approximately 300 ± 75 base pairs of C1-3A/TG1-3 repeats with a 3' G-rich single-stranded overhang.
source: In the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, telomeric DNA consists of approximately ~300 ± 75 base pairs of C1-3A/TG1-3 repeats with a 3' G-rich single-stranded overhang (Wellinger and Zakian, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Wellinger and Zakian, 2012, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Y'-elements are present as a tandem array of 0–4 copies at telomeres.
source: The Y'-elements, immediately internal to the telomeric repeats, are present as a tandem array of 0–4 copies, they fall into two major size classes, 6.7 kb Y'-long (Y'-L) and 5.2 kb Y'-short (Y'-S) (Chan and Tye, 1983a; Chan et al., 1983b).
evidence: This is cited from Chan and Tye, 1983a and Chan et al., 1983b, representing established structural information.

claim: Y'-elements fall into two major size classes: 6.7 kb Y'-long (Y'-L) and 5.2 kb Y'-short (Y'-S).
source: The Y'-elements, immediately internal to the telomeric repeats, are present as a tandem array of 0–4 copies, they fall into two major size classes, 6.7 kb Y'-long (Y'-L) and 5.2 kb Y'-short (Y'-S) (Chan and Tye, 1983a; Chan et al., 1983b).
evidence: This is cited from Chan and Tye, 1983a and Chan et al., 1983b, representing established structural information.

claim: Y'-elements are highly conserved with only ~2% divergence between strains.
source: Y'-elements are highly conserved with only ~2% divergence between strains (Louis and Haber, 1992).
evidence: This is cited from Louis and Haber, 1992, representing established knowledge about Y'-element conservation.

claim: One entire Y'-element contains two large open-reading frames (ORFs), an ARS consensus sequence (ACS), and a STAR element.
source: One entire Y'-element contains two large open-reading frames (ORFs), an ARS consensus sequence (ACS), and a STAR element (subtelomeric anti-silencing regions) consisting of binding sites for Tbf1 and Reb1 (Chan and Tye, 1983a; Chan et al., 1983b; Fourel et al., 1999; Louis and Haber, 1992).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources describing the structural features of Y'-elements.

claim: The X-element contains the 473 bp 'core X' sequence and the subtelomeric repeats (STRs) A, B, C, and D.
source: The X-element, a much more heterogeneous sequence abutting Y'-elements or telomeric repeats, contains the 473 bp 'core X' sequence and the subtelomeric repeats (STRs) A, B, C, and D (Louis and Haber, 1991; Louis et al., 1994).
evidence: This is cited from Louis and Haber, 1991 and Louis et al., 1994, representing established structural information.

claim: The 'core X' sequence is shared by all chromosomes.
source: The STRs are found in some chromosome ends, while the 'core X' sequence is shared by all chromosomes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about X-element distribution.

claim: Subtelomeric regions display high evolutionary plasticity and are rich in various structure variants such as reciprocal translocations, transpositions, novel insertions, deletions, and duplications.
source: Recent long-read sequencing shows that subtelomeric regions display high evolutionary plasticity and are rich in various structure variants such as reciprocal translocations, transpositions, novel insertions, deletions, and duplications (O'Donnell et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited from O'Donnell et al., 2023, representing recent findings from long-read sequencing studies.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, the telomerase holoenzyme consists of the reverse transcriptase Est2, the RNA template TLC1, and accessory factors Est1, Est3, Pop1/Pop6/Pop7 proteins.
source: In S. cerevisiae, the telomerase holoenzyme consists of the reverse transcriptase Est2, the RNA template TLC1, and accessory factors Est1, Est3, Pop1/Pop6/Pop7 proteins (Lemieux et al., 2016; Lendvay et al., 1996; Lundblad and Szostak, 1989; Singer and Gottschling, 1994).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources representing established knowledge about telomerase composition.

claim: In the absence of telomerase, homologous recombination can take place to replicate telomeres, resulting in telomerase-deficient 'survivors'.
source: In the absence of telomerase, homologous recombination can take place to replicate telomeres, resulting in telomerase-deficient 'survivors' (Lundblad and Blackburn, 1993; Teng and Zakian, 1999).
evidence: This is cited from Lundblad and Blackburn, 1993 and Teng and Zakian, 1999, representing established knowledge about alternative telomere maintenance.

claim: Survivors are broadly categorized into Type I and Type II based on distinct telomere structures.
source: These survivors are broadly categorized into Type I and Type II based on distinct telomere structures (Lundblad and Blackburn, 1993; Teng and Zakian, 1999).
evidence: This is cited from Lundblad and Blackburn, 1993 and Teng and Zakian, 1999, representing established classification of survivors.

claim: Type I survivors possess tandem amplified Y'-elements and very short TG1-3 tracts.
source: Type I survivors possess tandem amplified Y'-elements (both Y'-L and Y'-S) and very short TG1-3 tracts, indicating that Y'-elements serve as substrates for homologous recombination.
evidence: This is cited knowledge about Type I survivor characteristics, supported by references to Lundblad and Blackburn, 1993 and Teng and Zakian, 1999.

claim: Type II survivors display long heterogeneous TG1-3 tracts.
source: Type II survivors display long heterogeneous TG1-3 tracts.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Type II survivor characteristics.

claim: On solid medium, approximately 90% of the survivors are Type I, while 10% are Type II.
source: On solid medium, approximately 90% of the survivors are Type I, while 10% are Type II (Teng et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from Teng et al., 2000, representing established knowledge about survivor frequencies.

claim: In liquid culture, Type II survivors grow faster and eventually dominate the population.
source: However, in liquid culture, Type II survivors grow faster and eventually dominate the population (Teng and Zakian, 1999).
evidence: This is cited from Teng and Zakian, 1999, representing established knowledge about survivor dynamics.

claim: Type I survivors depend on Rad51, Rad54, Rad55, Rad57, and Pif1.
source: Type I survivors depend on Rad51, Rad54, Rad55, Rad57, and Pif1 (Chen et al., 2001; Hu et al., 2013; Le et al., 1999).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources representing established knowledge about genetic requirements for Type I survivors.

claim: The formation of Type II survivors requires the Mre11/Rad50/Xrs2 (MRX) complex, KEOPS complex, Rad59, Sgs1, and Rad6.
source: while the formation of Type II survivors requires the Mre11/Rad50/Xrs2 (MRX) complex, KEOPS complex, Rad59, Sgs1, and Rad6, most of which are critical for DNA resection (Chen et al., 2001; He et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2013; Johnson et al., 2001; Le et al., 1999; Huang et al., 2001; Nicolette et al., 2010; Teng et al., 2000; Wellinger and Zakian, 2012; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources representing established knowledge about genetic requirements for Type II survivors.

claim: In the SY12 strain, only the XVI-L telomere contained a single copy of the Y'-element, while all telomeres harbored X-elements.
source: The results revealed that, in the SY12 strain used in our study, only the XVI-L telomere contained a single copy of the Y'-element, while all telomeres harbored X-elements (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Southern blotting data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: As the number of chromosomes decreased in SYn strains, the frequency of Type II survivors gradually diminished, while Type I survivors became the predominant type.
source: Intriguingly, as the number of chromosomes decreased, the frequency of Type II survivors gradually diminished, while Type I survivors became the predominant type (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Southern blotting data in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Non-canonical survivors with distinct patterns from Type I or Type II emerged in SY9, SY10, SY11, SY12, and SY13 tlc1Δ strains.
source: Furthermore, non-canonical survivors with distinct patterns from Type I or Type II emerged in SY9 tlc1Δ (six chromosomes), SY10 tlc1Δ (five chromosomes), SY11 tlc1Δ (four chromosomes), SY12 tlc1Δ (three chromosomes), and SY13 tlc1Δ (two chromosomes) (Figure 1C and D indicated by triangles at the bottom of the panels).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Southern blotting data in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The ratio of survivor types is influenced by the number of chromosomes.
source: These findings suggest that the ratio of survivor types is influenced by the number of chromosomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that survivor type frequencies change with chromosome number.

claim: Among 50 SY12 tlc1Δ survivors, 16% exhibited the typical Type I telomere structure characterized by Y'-element amplification.
source: Among these survivors, eight clones (labeled in red, 16% of the survivors tested) exhibited the typical Type I telomere structure characterized by Y'-element amplification (Figure 2D and E and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Southern blotting data in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The emergence of Type I survivor in SY12 strain which only contain one Y'-element indicates that multiple Y'-elements in tandem are not strictly required for Type I formation.
source: The emergence of Type I survivor in SY12 strain which only contain one Y'-element indicates that multiple Y'-elements in tandem are not strictly required for Type I formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the observation of Type I survivors in SY12 with only one Y'-element.

claim: Among 50 SY12 tlc1Δ survivors, 2% displayed heterogeneous telomeric TG1-3 tracts indicating Type II survivors.
source: Clone 1 (labeled in orange, 2% of the survivors tested) displayed heterogeneous telomeric TG1-3 tracts (Figure 2D and E and Supplementary file 5), indicating it was a Type II survivor.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Southern blotting data in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Among 50 SY12 tlc1Δ survivors, 20% underwent intra-chromosomal circularization.
source: Notably, 10 of the examined clones (labeled in blue, 20% of the survivors tested) displayed no telomere signals associated with canonical Type I or II survivors (Figure 2D and E and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Southern blotting, PCR-mapping, and PFGE data.

claim: The three chromosomes in SY12 tlc1Δ-C1 cells had undergone intra-chromosomal fusions through microhomology-mediated end joining (MMEJ).
source: The results revealed that the three chromosomes in SY12 tlc1Δ-C1 cells had undergone intra-chromosomal fusions through microhomology-mediated end joining (MMEJ) (Wu et al., 2020), resulting in the formation of circular chromosomes (Figure 2F and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by PCR-sequencing data in Figure 2F and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Among 50 SY12 tlc1Δ survivors, 24% were designated as Type X survivors characterized by the absence of both Y'-amplification and superlong TG1-3 sequences.
source: Twelve clones of SY12 tlc1Δ survivors (labeled in green, 24% of the survivors tested) exhibited no Y'-telomere signals compared to SY12 cells but displayed different lengths of TG1-3 tracts (Figure 2D and E and Supplementary file 5). Due to their non-canonical telomere structures, characterized by the absence of both Y'- amplification and superlong TG1-3 sequences, we designated these SY12 tlc1Δ survivors (labeled in green, Figure 2D) as Type X.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Southern blotting data in Figure 2D and E.

claim: In Type X survivors, the Y'-elements had been eroded, leaving only the TG1-3 tracts at the very ends.
source: The newly emerged band at approximately 4.3 kb likely originated from the XVI-L telomere (indicated by the red arrow on the right in the panel) (Figure 2D), where the Y'-elements had been eroded, leaving only the TG1-3 tracts at the very ends (Figure 2A, right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Southern blotting and PCR-sequencing data.

claim: Type X survivors possess linear chromosomes with telomeres terminating in TG1-3 repeats, while the Y'-element has been eroded.
source: These data indicated that Type X survivors possess linear chromosomes with telomeres terminating in TG1-3 repeats, while the Y'-element has been eroded (Figure 2A, right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by PCR-sequencing and Southern blotting data.

claim: The Y'-element is not essential for yeast cell viability.
source: Consistently, no Y' signals were detected in these 12 Type X survivors (labeled in green, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the Y'-element has not been translocated to other telomeres and is not essential for yeast cell viability.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the observation that Type X survivors lacking Y'-elements are viable.

claim: Rad52 is not strictly required for survivor generation in the SY12 strain in liquid culture.
source: The results showed double deletion of TLC1 and RAD52 in SY12 strain could slightly accelerate senescence, and SY12 tlc1Δ rad52Δ survivors could be generated but took much longer to recover than the SY12 tlc1Δ survivors (Figure 2—figure supplement 7A), suggesting that Rad52 is not strictly required for survivor generation in the SY12 strain in liquid.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cell viability assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 7A.

claim: The formation of circular survivors in the SY12 tlc1Δ rad52Δ strain is mediated by MMEJ, not RAD52 mediated pathways.
source: We conclude that the formation of circular survivors in the SY12 tlc1Δ rad52Δ strain is mediated by MMEJ as observed in the SY14 tlc1Δ rad52Δ strain (Wu et al., 2020), but not RAD52 mediate pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Southern blotting data showing circular survivors in rad52Δ background.

claim: The formation of the Type X survivor depends on Rad50-mediated Type II pathway.
source: In contrast, no Type X survivor was detected in the SY12 tlc1Δ rad50Δ strain (Figure 2—figure supplement 8B). These data suggest that the formation of the Type X survivor depends on Rad50-mediated Type II pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Southern blotting data showing absence of Type X survivors in rad50Δ background.

claim: The SY12YΔ, SY12XYΔ, and SY12XYΔ+Y cells exhibited the same cell morphology as the parental strains SY12 and BY4742.
source: The SY12YΔ, SY12XYΔ, and SY12XYΔ+Y cells, cultured in YPD medium at 30°C, exhibited the same cell morphology as the parental strains SY12 and BY4742 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by DIC microscopy images in Figure 3C.

claim: SY12YΔ, SY12XYΔ, and SY12XYΔ+Y strains grew robustly on solid medium over 61 re-streaks.
source: Similar to the SY12 strain, the progeny colonies of SY12YΔ, SY12XYΔ, and SY12XYΔ+Y grew robustly on solid medium (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by growth assay data in Figure 3D.

claim: SY12YΔ, SY12XYΔ, and SY12XYΔ+Y cells exhibited growth rates comparable to those of SY12 and BY4742 cells in liquid medium.
source: Moreover, SY12YΔ, SY12XYΔ, and SY12XYΔ+Y cells exhibited growth rates comparable to those of SY12 and BY4742 cells in liquid medium (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by growth curve data in Figure 3E.

claim: SY12YΔ, SY12XYΔ, and SY12XYΔ+Y had the same 1C and 2C DNA content as wild-type cells.
source: Fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) analysis revealed that SY12YΔ, SY12XYΔ, and SY12XYΔ+Y had the same 1C and 2C DNA content as wild-type cells (Figure 3F), indicating that the X- and Y'-elements are not necessary for cell proliferation under normal conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by FACS data in Figure 3F.

claim: X- and Y'-elements are not necessary for cell proliferation under normal conditions.
source: Fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) analysis revealed that SY12YΔ, SY12XYΔ, and SY12XYΔ+Y had the same 1C and 2C DNA content as wild-type cells (Figure 3F), indicating that the X- and Y'-elements are not necessary for cell proliferation under normal conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on FACS and growth data.

claim: X- and Y'-elements are dispensable for cellular responses to cold or heat treatment and DNA damage challenges.
source: These results indicate that the X- and Y'-elements are dispensable for cellular responses to cold or heat treatment and DNA damage challenges, consistent with a recent study of 'synthetic yeast genome project', namely Sc2.0, showing that thousands of genome-wide edits, including the deletion of subtelomeric repetitive sequences, deletion of introns, and relocation of tRNAs genes, yielded a strain that displays comparable growth with wild-type strain (Richardson et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by serial dilution assay data in Figure 3G.

claim: SY12YΔ, SY12XYΔ, and SY12XYΔ+Y cells maintained stable telomeres at a length of approximately 300 bp, comparable to that in SY12 cells.
source: Southern blotting assay revealed that SY12YΔ, SY12XYΔ, and SY12XYΔ+Y cells maintained stable telomeres at a length of approximately 300 bp, comparable to that in SY12 cells (Figure 4A), indicating that the X- and Y'-elements are not required for telomere length regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Southern blotting data in Figure 4A.

claim: X- and Y'-elements are not required for telomere length regulation.
source: Southern blotting assay revealed that SY12YΔ, SY12XYΔ, and SY12XYΔ+Y cells maintained stable telomeres at a length of approximately 300 bp, comparable to that in SY12 cells (Figure 4A), indicating that the X- and Y'-elements are not required for telomere length regulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on Southern blotting data.

claim: Telomere silencing remains effective in the absence of X-and Y'-elements.
source: We then performed real-time RT-PCR to quantify the expression of the MPH3 and HSP32 genes, located near the subtelomeric region of X-R (X-only end) and XVI-L (X-Y' end), respectively (Figure 4B), and found that the increase of the MPH3 or HSP32 expression upon SIR2 deletion in SY12YΔ, SY12XYΔ, and SY12XYΔ+Y strains was more significant than that in the BY4742 or the SY12 strain, indicating that telomere silencing remains effective in the absence of X-and Y'-elements (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4B.

claim: X- and Y'-elements function as modulators of TPE (telomere position effect).
source: These findings align with previous studies showing that telomeres without an X- or Y'-element exert a position effect on the transcription of neighboring genes (Aparicio et al., 1991), and that X- and Y'-elements function as modulators of TPE (Fourel et al., 1999; Lebrun et al., 2001; Ottaviani et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources representing established knowledge about the role of subtelomeric elements in TPE.

claim: Y'-elements are not strictly required for the formation of Type II survivors.
source: Overall, these findings indicate that Y'-elements are not strictly required for Type II survivor formation (Churikov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the observation of Type II survivors in SY12YΔ tlc1Δ strain.

claim: Among 50 SY12YΔ tlc1Δ survivors, 4% were Type II survivors.
source: Two clones (labeled in orange, 4% of the survivors tested) displayed heterogeneous telomere tracts (Figure 5C and D and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Southern blotting data in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Among 50 SY12YΔ tlc1Δ survivors, 52% were circular survivors.
source: Twenty-six clones (labeled in blue, 52% of the survivors tested) exhibited patterns identical to that of the SY12 tlc1Δ circular survivors (Figures 5C and D and 2D and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Southern blotting data in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Survivor formation in SY12YΔ tlc1Δ rad52Δ cells does not strictly rely on the homologous recombination.
source: Southern blotting assay confirmed that most of the recovered clones were circular survivors, and two were uncharacterized survivors (clones 9 and 16, labeled in black, Figure 5—figure supplement 3B), suggesting that survivor formation in SY12YΔ tlc1Δ rad52Δ cells does not strictly rely on the homologous recombination.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Southern blotting data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: X-elements are not strictly necessary for survivor generation.
source: Overall, these data suggest that X-elements are not strictly necessary for survivor formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the observation of survivors in SY12XYΔ+Y and SY12XYΔ tlc1Δ strains.

claim: Among 50 SY12XYΔ+Y tlc1Δ survivors, 44% underwent chromosomal circularization.
source: Among the SY12XYΔ+Y survivors analyzed, 22 clones underwent chromosomal circularization (labeled in blue, 44% of the survivors tested, Figure 6A and C and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Southern blotting data in Figure 6A and C.

claim: Among 50 SY12XYΔ+Y tlc1Δ survivors, 14% utilized the Type II recombination pathway.
source: Additionally, seven clones utilized the Type II recombination pathway and exhibited heterogeneous telomeric TG1-3 tracts (labeled in orange, 14% of the survivors tested, Figure 6A and C and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Southern blotting data in Figure 6A and C.

claim: No Type I survivors were generated in SY12XYΔ+Y tlc1Δ survivors even though there is a Y'-element.
source: While even though there is a Y'-element, no Type I survivors were generated in SY12XYΔ+Y tlc1Δ survivors (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Southern blotting data in Figure 6A.

claim: The short TG1-3 repeats located centromere-proximal to the Y'-elements play a crucial role in strand invasion and subsequent Y'-recombination.
source: We speculated that the short TG1-3 repeats located centromere-proximal to the Y'-elements play a crucial role in strand invasion and subsequent Y'-recombination. This speculation is consistent with a previous report stating that Type I events are virtually absent in the yeast strain Y55, which lacks TG1-3 repeats centromere-proximal to the Y'-element (Huang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Huang et al., 2001.

claim: Among 50 SY12XYΔ tlc1Δ survivors, 48% displayed a 'circular survivor' pattern.
source: Among the SY12XYΔ survivors, 24 displayed a 'circular survivor' pattern (labeled in blue, 48% of the survivors tested, Figure 6B and E and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Southern blotting data in Figure 6B and E.

claim: Among 50 SY12XYΔ tlc1Δ survivors, 8% harbored Type II telomere structure.
source: Also, 4 of 50 survivors harbored Type II telomere structure (labeled in orange, 8% of the survivors tested, Figure 6B and E and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Southern blotting data in Figure 6B and E.

claim: Rad52 is not strictly required for the formation of circular survivors in SY12XYΔ tlc1Δ rad52Δ and SY12XYΔ+Y tlc1Δ rad52Δ strains.
source: Like in SY12 tlc1Δ cells, Rad52 is not strictly required for the formation of circular survivors in SY12XYΔ tlc1Δ rad52Δ and SY12XYΔ+Y tlc1Δ rad52Δ strains (Figure 6—figure supplement 6A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cell viability and Southern blotting data in Figure 6—figure supplement 6A and B.

claim: Type I-specific mechanisms still contribute to the survivor formation even in the Y'-less strain SY12XYΔ.
source: Accordingly, the ratio of Type II survivor in SY12XYΔ tlc1Δ rad51Δ was (32% of the survivors tested, Figure 6—figure supplement 7B and Supplementary file 5) was higher than SY12XYΔ tlc1Δ strain (8% of the survivors tested, Figure 6E and Supplementary file 5), suggesting that Type I-specific mechanisms still contribute to the survivor formation even in the Y'-less strain SY12XYΔ.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Southern blotting data comparing rad51Δ and wild-type backgrounds.

claim: X-elements, as well as Y'-elements, are not essential for the generation of Type II survivors.
source: Collectively, the aforementioned data suggest that X-elements, as well as Y'-elements, are not essential for the generation of Type II survivors.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the observation of Type II survivors in strains lacking these elements.

claim: Subtelomeric X- and Y'-elements might be considered as evolutionary 'fossils' in the S. cerevisiae genome.
source: Therefore, subtelomeric X- and Y'-elements might be considered as evolutionary 'fossils' in the S. cerevisiae genome, and their elimination has little impact on telomere essential functions and genome stability.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the findings that these elements are dispensable.

claim: The elimination of X- and Y'-elements has little impact on telomere essential functions and genome stability.
source: Therefore, subtelomeric X- and Y'-elements might be considered as evolutionary 'fossils' in the S. cerevisiae genome, and their elimination has little impact on telomere essential functions and genome stability.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the experimental data showing normal telomere function in strains lacking these elements.

claim: Multiple Y'-elements in tandem are not strictly required for Type I recombination.
source: Type I survivors emerged in SY12 strain, indicating that multiple Y'-elements in tandem are not strictly required for Type I recombination (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by the observation of Type I survivors in SY12 with only one Y'-element.

claim: The acquisition of Y'-elements is not a prerequisite for Type II survivor formation.
source: Interestingly, the telomerase-null SY12YΔ and SY12XYΔ cells, lacking Y'-elements, failed to generate Type I survivors but could generate Type II survivors, indicating that the acquisition of Y'-elements is not a prerequisite for Type II survivor formation (Figures 5C and 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by the observation of Type II survivors in strains lacking Y'-elements.

claim: Type I and Type II survivors form independently.
source: These observations support the notion that Type I and Type II survivors form independently, although both may utilize a common alternative telomere-lengthening pathway (Kockler et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Kockler et al., 2021 and the experimental observations.

claim: A smaller number of telomeres provides fewer recombination donors and acceptors, resulting in less efficient inter-chromosomal homologous recombination.
source: First, a smaller number of telomeres provides fewer recombination donors and acceptors, resulting in less efficient inter-chromosomal homologous recombination (e.g., TG1-3 tracts recombination or Y'-element acquisition).
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion to explain the increased frequency of circular survivors in strains with fewer chromosomes.

claim: Survivors with circular chromosomes do not encounter end-replication problems and therefore exhibit greater stability.
source: Second, the continuously shortened telomeres of linear chromosomes may trigger another round of senescence, while survivors with circular chromosomes do not encounter end-replication problems and therefore exhibit greater stability.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion to explain the prevalence of circular survivors.

claim: The presence of homologous sequences at both chromosome ends appears to be a minimum requirement for microhomology-mediated intra-chromosomal end-to-end fusion.
source: Third, the presence of homologous sequences at both chromosome ends appears to be a minimum requirement for microhomology-mediated intra-chromosomal end-to-end fusion.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion based on the mechanism of MMEJ.

claim: In telomerase-null cells with eroded chromosome ends, stochastic repair mechanisms such as homologous recombination, microhomology-mediated end joining, and inter- and intra-chromosomal fusions operate simultaneously.
source: However, we can speculate that in telomerase-null cells with eroded chromosome ends, stochastic repair mechanisms such as homologous recombination, microhomology-mediated end joining, and inter- and intra-chromosomal fusions operate simultaneously.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion based on the diverse survivor types observed.

claim: S. cerevisiae and S. pombe are separated by approximately 1 Gya (billion years ago) according to molecular-clock analyses.
source: S. cerevisiae (budding yeast) and Schizosaccharomyces pombe (fission yeast) are the most commonly used laboratory systems, separated by approximately 1 Gya (billion years ago) according to molecular-clock analyses (Hedges, 2002).
evidence: This is cited from Hedges, 2002, representing established knowledge about yeast evolution.

claim: Haploid S. cerevisiae contains 16 chromosomes, while S. pombe has only 3 chromosomes.
source: Despite both species having genomes are both over 12 megabases in length, haploid S. cerevisiae contains 16 chromosomes, while S. pombe has only 3 chromosomes (Forsburg, 2005).
evidence: This is cited from Forsburg, 2005, representing established knowledge about yeast genome structure.

claim: A lower chromosome number increases the likelihood of recovering survivors containing circular chromosomes.
source: In our research, some SY12 tlc1Δ cells, which have three chromosomes, also bypassed senescence by circularizing their chromosomes (Figure 2D), suggesting that a lower chromosome number increases the likelihood of recovering survivors containing circular chromosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by the observation of circular survivors in SY12 and comparison with other strains.

claim: Subtelomeric region amplification mediated by recombination and/or transposition may represent ancient telomere maintenance mechanisms predating the evolution of telomerase.
source: These findings suggest that subtelomeric region amplification mediated by recombination and/or transposition may represent ancient telomere maintenance mechanisms predating the evolution of telomerase (de Lange, 2004).
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to de Lange, 2004.

claim: The SY12YΔ, SY12XYΔ, and SY12XYΔ+Y strains, with their simplified telomere structures, are valuable resources for telomere biology research.
source: Thus, the SY12YΔ, SY12XYΔ, and SY12XYΔ+Y strains established in this study, with their simplified telomere structures, are valuable resources for telomere biology research.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the characterization of these strains.

source: In wild-type yeast strain BY4742, there are 8 Y'-S and 11 Y'-L elements at the 32 telomere loci.

source: Additionally, each telomere locus contains one X-element.

claim: The 'core X' sequence acts as a protosilencer.
source: The 'core X' sequence consists of an ACS element and, in most cases, an Abf1 binding site (Louis, 1995), and acts as a protosilencer (Lebrun et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from Lebrun et al., 2001, representing established knowledge about X-element function.

claim: STRs and Y'-STAR possess anti-silencing properties that limit the spreading of heterochromatin.
source: In contrast, STRs and Y'-STAR possess anti-silencing properties that limit the spreading of heterochromatin (Fourel et al., 1999).

source: Interestingly, a previous study demonstrated that telomeres with Χ-only ends (containing only X-elements) were more efficiently elongated compared to those with X-Y' ends (containing both X- and Y'-elements) in tel1Δ rif1Δ strains (Craven and Petes, 1999).
evidence: This is cited from Craven and Petes, 1999, representing previous findings about X-element effects on telomere elongation.

source: Moreover, subtelomeric elements (including X-elements) and associated factors like Reb1 and Tbf1 antagonize telomere anchoring at the nuclear envelope (Hediger et al., 2006).
